Title: Dithiol cross-linked polynorbornene-based anion-exchange membranes with high hydroxide conductivity and alkaline stability

Sections.name: Introduction
content: Hydrogen is widely recognized as an environmentally friendly energy carrier, and its preparation and utilization are of significant importance for global decarbonization efforts [1]. Electrolysis of water is currently the most common method for generating “green-hydrogen” [2], with three primary techniques in use: alkaline water electrolysis (AWE), proton-exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), and anion-exchange membrane water electrolysis (AEMWE) []. However, AWE suffers from low efficiency, safety concerns regarding cathode and anode separators, and the inability to produce pressurized hydrogen required for automotive applications. PEMWE, on the other hand, boasts a high current density and can produce pressurized hydrogen, but the reliance on electrocatalysts based on rare elements such as iridium and platinum leads to high equipment costs. Therefore, AEMWE, which can use non-precious metal catalysts and have fast cathode reaction kinetics, has emerged as an attractive green method for hydrogen production [1,3,]. The critical components of AEMWEs are anion exchange membranes (AEMs), which consist of polymeric backbones, cations attached to the backbone via covalent bonds, and free anions [9].

The conductivity and stability of AEMs play a crucial role in determining the current density and durability of AEMWE systems. To improve the durability of AEMWEs, many researchers have investigated the chemical stability of AEMs, including the stability of both polymer backbones and organic cations [4,7,10]. However, compared to the cation effect, the impact of AEM polymeric backbones on AEM properties is relatively unexplored [11]. Previous studies have shown that aryl ether linkages in polymer backbones (such as polysulfone and poly(arylene ether) backbones) are susceptible to degradation at high pH conditions, leading to the development of AEMs with C–C bond backbones such as polyethylene, polystyrene, polyarylene, and polynorbornene []. Nevertheless, polyethylene derivatives are challenging to dissolve in organic solvents, and their AEMs can only be prepared through thermal pressing, limiting their large-scale production [22]. Additionally, adsorption of aromatic groups onto electrocatalysts can have negative impacts on device performance [23]. In recent years, polynorbornene (PNB) backbones have gained popularity in the AEM community due to their excellent thermal and chemical stability as well as their good film-forming properties [].

The polymerization of norbornenes (NBs) can be accomplished through two different pathways depending on the catalysts used: ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) and vinylic-addition polymerization (VA) [27,28]. The ROMP-PNB-based AEMs have the advantages of ease of synthesis and functionalization, while cross-linking or backbone-hydrogenation are usually required to improve mechanical strength of the membranes [25,]. For example, Coates et al. [35] prepared ROMP-PNB-based AEMs by reactive casting of trimethylammonium-functionalized NB moieties with dicyclopentadiene cross-linking. A similar strategy was applied to prepare cross-linked transition-metal-functionalized ROMP-PNB-AEMs [29,36,37]. Kohl et al. [25] prepared a series of hydrogenated cross-linked AEMs which were synthesized on the basis of the ROMP of alkyl-substituted NB derivatives. The resulting AEMs possessed very high ion exchange capacities (IECs) ranging from 2.31 to 4.73 mequiv/g and retained mechanical integrity in water. In addition, Noonan et al. [38] reported ROMP-PNB-based AEMs with alkaline-stable tetrakisdialkylaminophosphonium cations and well-defined block structures.

On the other hand, VA-PNB-based AEMs tend to display high thermal stability, better mechanical properties, and are more chemically inert than their ROMP-PNB counterparts due to their rigid, saturated polymer backbones. VA-PNBs have higher glass-transition temperature (T _{g}) due to the retention of the rigid bicyclic norbornane motifs along the polymer backbones [27]. Kohl et al. [39,40] used alkyl-halogen-substituted norbornene to copolymerize with alkyl-substituted norbornene, followed by subsequent diamine crosslinking and quaternization to give rise to a series of high-performance VA-PNB-AEMs. The AEMs have high hydroxide conductivity of 198 mS/cm at 80 °C and no significant conductivity drop over 1000 h of aging in 1 M NaOH at 80 °C. After mechanical reinforcement by porous polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), the VA-PNB-AEMs and anion-exchange ionomers were assembled into anion-exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) with high peak power density (3.4 W/cm^{2}) and stable device performance for over 2000 h [24,41,42]. Moreover, the ionic group distribution can also be controlled during the VA-polymerization process as statistical or multiblock copolymers, so that the microphase separation structures can be tuned [43]. All of these pioneered reports highlighted the promising features of using VA-PNBs as high-performance AEM backbones. However, the reported NB monomers for VA-PNB-based AEMs are limited to alkyl-substituted NB and alkyl-halogen-substituted NB derivatives. This is likely due to the relatively narrow monomer scope of VA polymerization reactions [27]. The limited monomer scope also leads to limited cross-linking methods (diamine Menshutkin reactions only), thus more research is needed to improve monomer derivatization for VA-PNB-based AEMs.

5-Vinyl-2-norbornene (VNB), an inexpensive commercially available reagent, is capable of undergoing vinylic-addition copolymerization via the NB-type double bonds, while leaving the terminal vinyl groups unreacted [44]. Therefore, the VA-PNBs derived from VNB monomers have plenty of terminal alkenes for further functionalized reactions, such as thiol-ene click reactions. In fact, thiol-ene click chemistry is an efficient and stable cross-linking strategy to control the water uptake and to improve the AEM performance [45]. Hickner et al. [46] used this method to prepare dithiol-cross-linked quaternary ammonium functionalized poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide)s (PPO) based AEMs with high hydroxide conductivities (up to 200 mS/cm at 80 °C) and moderate alkaline stability. In this study, it is hypothesized that by copolymerizing alkyl-halogen-substituted NBs with VNB through VA polymerization, followed by photo-induced thiol-ene click cross-linking and quaternization, a series of VA-PNB-AEMs with excellent structural tunability can be obtained. The resultant AEMs exhibit ultrahigh IECs and hydroxide conductivities, as well as good alkaline and thermal stability, while still maintaining low water absorption and swelling ratios.

content.name: Materials
content: Tris(dibenzylideneacetone)dipalladium (Pd_{2}(dba)_{3}), tricyclohexylphosphine (PCy_{3}), 3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol, 1,6-hexanedithiol, phenylbis(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide, and trimethylamine aqueous solution were purchased from Energy Chemical Co., Shanghai, China. Lithium ion diethyl ether tetrakis(pentafluorophenyl)boranuide (Li[FABA]) was purchased from Aladdin Co., Ltd. Shanghai, China. 6-Bromo-1-hexene was purchased from J&K Scientific Co., Beijing, China. Silver nitrate and potassium nitrate were purchased from Innochem Co., Ltd. Beijing, China. Potassium hydroxide, sodium bicarbonate, and sodium chloride were purchased from Beijing Chemical Works. Methanol and chloroform were purchased from Concord Inc., Tianjin, China. All abovementioned chemicals were used as received without further purification.

5-Vinyl-2-norbornene (VNB) was purchased from Energy Chemical Co., Shanghai, China. which was distilled in potassium carbonate before use. Toluene was dried in the solvent purification system before use. Cyclopentadiene (CPD) was obtained by dicyclopentadiene (DCPD) cracking in potassium carbonate in a nitrogen atmosphere at 230 °C and DCPD was purchased from Energy Chemical Co., Shanghai, China.

content.name: Polymer synthesis
content: Synthesis of BrNB monomer. BrNB was synthesized according to the literature procedures [43]. CPD (150 mmol) and 6-bromo-1-hexene (300 mmol) were combined in a sealed 200 mL pressure vessel equipped with a magnetic stir bar in a nitrogen atmosphere. The mixture was heated to 200 °C for 48 h in a sand bath. After the reaction, the solution was cooled to room temperature, then distilled under reduced pressure to obtain the product (42% yield, boiling point = 114–116 °C).

Synthesis of the copolymers. Copolymers were synthesized according to the literature procedures [47,48]. The copolymerization was performed in a dry glovebox under a nitrogen atmosphere. First, the activated catalyst solution was prepared by addition of toluene (3.0 mL) to Pd_{2}(dba)_{3} 6.9 mg (0.0075 mmol), PCy_{3} 8.4 mg (0.030 mmol), Li[FABA] 22.8 mg (0.030 mmol) in a 20 mL bottle with a magnetic stirring bar, and then stirred at room temperature for 1 h. Subsequently, the activated catalyst solution was filtered and injected into the toluene solution containing BrNB (1.5–2.0 mmol) and VNB (1.5–1.0 mmol), and the polymerization was carried out at room temperature for 12 h. After the reaction, the bottle was moved outside the glove box. The polymer solution was precipitated in methanol and collected by filtration. The desired polymers (V–x) were obtained after drying under vacuum, x represents the feeding ratio of BrNB and VNB (89%–99% yield).

content.name: Membrane preparation and ion exchange
content: The membranes were prepared by two different processes. First, the synthesized V-x copolymer, dithiol and photo-initiator (phenylbis(2,4,6-trimethylbenzoyl)phosphine oxide) were mixed in chloroform, and stirred at room temperature until completely dissolved. Then the obtained solution was poured into the mold, and the cross-linking reaction was carried out and solvents were evaporated simultaneously under the conditions of UV irradiation (365 nm) for 30 min to obtain the cross-linked membranes. Subsequently, the cross-linked membranes were quaternized by immersion in 35 wt% aqueous trimethylamine solution for 48 h at room temperature to obtain the membranes in the Br^{−} form. The membranes denoted as V-x-O-y or V-x-H-y, where x represents the molar ratio of BrNB to VNB; y represents the feeding ratio of sulfydryl and double bond; O represents that the cross-linking agent is 3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol; H represents that the cross-linking agent is 1,6-hexanedithiol. The thickness range of the prepared membranes were 40–50 μm. The membranes in the HCO_{3} ^{−} form was obtained by immersing in 1 M NaHCO_{3} solution for 24 h and washing with DI water for three times.

content.name: Characterization
content: Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FT-IR). FT-IR spectra were collected in the range of 4000–650 cm^{−1} with the number of scans per spectrum of 32 and the spectrum resolution of 4 cm^{−1} (Thermo Fisher Nicolet 6700).
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR). ^{1}H NMR spectra were obtained using CDCl_{3} solvents with the number of scans per spectrum of 16 (Bruker Avance III 400 HD or Bruker Avance 400).

Gel Permeation Chromatography (GPC). Molecular weights (M _{n} and M _{w}) and polydispersity (Đ) were measured by GPC in THF (40 °C) mobile phase based on narrowly distributed polystyrene (PS) standard with a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min (Agilent 1260 Infinity II).

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM). SEM imaging with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) was performed to observe the morphology and distribution of elements of the as-prepared membranes with gold sputtering (5 kV of the accelerated voltage) (Hitachi S-4800).

Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM). The V-2-H-1 crosslinked membrane was embedded at 70 °C for 10 h, and was ultra-thin sectioned to prepare the thin slice at ambient temperature (ca. 20 °C) considering its high T _{g}. The morphology of the slices mounted on the carbon-coated copper grids was observed by a TEM (Hitachi, HT7700) under the operation voltage of 100 kV.
Thermal Gravimetric Analyzer (TGA). The thermal stabilities of the polymers were determined by using a TGA 8000 (PerkinElmer) from 50 °C to 650 °C at a rate of 20 °C/min under a nitrogen atmosphere.

Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC). Melting temperatures (T _{m}) and glass-transition temperature (T _{g}) of the polymers were determined by using a TA Q200 DSC under a nitrogen atmosphere refer to the literature [22]. The samples were heated to 200 °C at a rate of 10 °C per minute.

The fractions of free water (N _{free}) and bound water (N _{bound}) were determined by using a TA Q8500 DSC under a nitrogen atmosphere. The test methods and calculation method refer to the literature [26]. The membrane samples were fully hydrated by soaking in deionized water for one week. After the water on the membrane surface was dabbed off, a 3–5 mg sample was quickly sealed in an aluminum pan. The sample was cooled to −50 °C and then heated to 30 °C at a rate of 5 °C/min under nitrogen atmosphere.

Ion Exchange Capacity (IEC). IEC was determined by Mohr titration using an ion meter PXSJ-216F (INESA Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China) as previously reported [22]. The IEC numbers were calculated according to the average of three samples.
Water Uptake (WU) and Swelling Ratio (SR). WU and SR values were calculated as previously reported [22].

Small Angle X-ray Scattering (SAXS). The microphase separation of dry membranes in the Br^{−}- and I^{−}-form were analyzed by SAXS at room temperature as previously reported [22]. The sample-to-detector distances were 2501 mm. The two-dimensional (2-D) SAXS patterns were collected for an image acquisition time of 1200 s. 1-D intensity profiles were integrated from the background-corrected 2-D SAXS patterns.

Bicarbonate conductivity at room temperature. The in-plane bicarbonate conductivity of the membranes was measured by four-probe electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) as previously reported [22]. The HCO_{3} ^{−} conductivity was obtained according to the average of three samples.

Hydroxide conductivity. A similar set-up was adopted from literature to measure “true hydroxide conductivities” under humidified conditions [22,49,50]. The operating temperatures from 40 to 90 °C while maintaining RH (Fig. S6).
Mechanical properties. The mechanical properties of the Dumbbell shape samples were repeated 5 times with a strain rate of 20 mm/min.

Alkaline stability. The as-prepared membrane samples were soaked in an aqueous 1 M KOH solution at 80 °C for over 50 days. At specific time intervals (every five days), HCO_{3} ^{−} conductivities were obtained as the average of three samples. The changes of IECs and FT-IR after the alkaline stability studies were also recorded.

Alkaline water electrolysis. The MEA was prepared through the catalyst-coated substrate (CCS) technique as previously reported [22]. The HER and OER catalyst layers were bought from Dioxide Materials [51]. 1.0 M or 0.1 M KOH was all studied for AEMWE performance from 1.3 V at 40 °C–80 °C using a battery test station (SS-L3010SPD).

Sections.name: Results and discussion
content: A three-component catalytic system, consisting of Pd_{2}(dba)_{3}, PCy_{3}, and Li[FABA] [47,48], was employed to synthesize copolymers of alkyl-bromide-substituted norbornene (BrNB) and 5-vinyl-2-norbornene (VNB) with the aim of achieving high contents of both alkyl-bromides for sequential quaternization and terminal alkenes for sequential thiol-ene cross-linking (Scheme 1 ). In this system, Pd_{2}(dba)_{3} was used as the pre-catalyst, PCy_{3} as the ligand, and Li[FABA] as the counter-anion cocatalyst [52]. Phosphine was included to stabilize the active catalytic centers, and the lithium cocatalyst played a role in activating the pre-catalyst. The Pd/Li/PCy_{3} ratio was 1/2/2, and the overall monomer concentration was 0.5 M in toluene. The copolymerization reactions were allowed to proceed for 12 h, and the yields, the number average molecular weights (M _{n}), and polydispersity (Đ) of the resulting copolymers were determined by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) analysis (Table 1 and Fig. S1). The copolymers are denoted as V-x, where x represents the feeding ratio of BrNB and VNB (x = n/m). The GPC analysis revealed the M _{n} of copolymers V-1, V-1.5, and V-2 as 57.0, 44.3, and 40.1 kDa, respectively. The yield and M _{n} of the copolymerization decreased with increasing ratio of BrNB to VNB, while the Đ increased, likely due to the influence of bromine from the BrNB monomer. The proton nuclear magnetic resonance (^{1}H NMR) spectra of copolymers V-1, V-1.5, and V-2 confirmed that the monomer ratios in the copolymers were the same as the feeding ratios (Figs. S12–S14).

Copolymers V-x were then cross-linked using 3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol or 1,6-hexanedithiol under UV irradiation at varying cross-linker concentrations at a given molar fraction of dithiol with respect to the total moles of VNB monomer in the copolymer (Scheme 2 ). Photo-cross-linking was carried out during solvent evaporation (reactive casting). The membranes were then aminated through immersion in a trimethylamine solution to obtain Br^{−} form membranes denoted as V-x-O-y or V-x-H-y, where O represents using the 3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol crosslinking agent, H represents using the 1,6-hexanedithiol crosslinking agent, and y represents the feeding molar ratio of thiols (–SH) and terminal alkenes from the copolymers (y = 2p/m).

The photographs of V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 are presented in Fig. 1 , showing smooth and transparent membrane surfaces with good flexibility. The scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of V-1.5-H-1 also show that the microscopic shape of the membranes is uniform and flat (Fig. S2). In addition, the energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis revealed the uniform distribution of the Br, N, and S elements within the membranes (Figs. S3 and S4). The Fourier transform infrared (FT-IR) spectra of copolymers V-x and their corresponding dithiol-cross-linked AEMs are shown in Fig. 2 and Fig. S5. The characteristic peaks at about 990 cm^{−1} of the terminal alkenes in the copolymers nearly disappeared after crosslinking.

The detailed properties of the cross-linked VA-PNB-AEMs are listed in Table 2 . When using both the relatively hydrophilic cross-linker (3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol) and the hydrophobic cross-linker (1,6-hexanedithiol), the resultant AEMs have high IECs (up to 2.97 mmol Cl^{−}/g), which was attributed to the high percentage of BrNB monomer in the V-x copolymers. The IEC values obtained by Mohr titration were lower than the IECs obtained by ^{1}H NMR analysis when the VNB contents were relatively high (x = n/m = 1 in V-1-O-0.6 and V-1-O-0.9), possibly demonstrating incomplete quaternization. However, when the x value increased, both ^{1}H NMR analysis and Mohr titration methods gave similar IEC values (such as V-2-H-1 and V-2-O-1), indicating quantitative conversion from bromoalkyl end-groups to the quaternary ammonium cations. Despite the high IECs, the water uptake (WU) and swelling ratio (SR) values of the membranes were low, indicating effective dithiol cross-linking with the terminal alkenes derived from VNB monomers. Thus, the trade-off between the dimensional stability of AEMs and high IECs was solved by the efficient thiol-ene cross-link strategy [46]. The HCO_{3} ^{−} ionic conductivities of V-1.5-O-1 and V-2-O-1 AEMs were above 10 mS/cm at room temperature, and that of V-2-H-1 was even higher (12.6 mS/cm), which was attributed to the high IEC. The hydration number (λ) of AEMs was between 6.0 –10.9, which was comparable to the previously reported values of the diamine-cross-linked VA-PNB-AEMs [39].

The major advantage of dithiol-cross-link over traditional diamine-cross-link is that the dithiol-cross-link contents, the ionic contents, and the hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity of the cross-linkers can be independently tuned. For example, by comparing V-1-O-0.6 and V-1-O-0.9 membranes, the latter one has higher dithiol-cross-link density, thus with lower water uptake (WU) and swelling ratio (SR). Their relatively low HCO_{3} ^{−} conductivities were attributed to the low ionic concentration derived from V-1 precursors, which resulted in a lower concentration of quaternary ammonium cations. Increasing the BrNB/VNB ratio to 1.5–2 and using equal thiol-alkene equivalents resulted in the V-1.5-O-1 and V-2-O-1 membranes. Satisfyingly, both membranes had high IECs, high ionic conductivities, and smooth surfaces, yet with relatively high WU. To further regulate the WU and dimensional stability of the AEMs, all-carbon 1,6-hexanedithiol was then used as the cross-linking agent. The V-1.5-H-1 and V-2-H-1 membranes were as smooth and transparent as the V-1.5-O-1 and V-2-O-1 membranes. Both the V-2-O-1 and V-2-H-1 had similarly high IECs of around 3 mmol Cl^{−}/g, while the one with the hydrophobic cross-linker (i.e., V-2-H-1) has better water uptake control, thus leading to the highest ionic conductivity among the dithiol-cross-linked VA-PNB-AEMs (Table 2).

The hydroxide conductivities are more relevant to the current density of the AEM-assembled water electrolyzers (AEMWEs). The “true hydroxide conductivities” of the AEMs were measured using an in situ de-carbonation protocol under direct current and high humidity conditions (relative humidity (RH) > 98%, Fig. 3 ) [49,50]. The results showed that the hydroxide conductivities of all membranes increased with temperatures. V-1.5-O-1 and V-2-O-1 membranes exhibited significantly higher hydroxide conductivities compared to V-1-O-0.6 and V-1-O-0.9 membranes, which can be attributed to the higher IEC. V-1.5-O-1 had significantly higher hydroxide conductivity compared to V-2-O-1, despite having lower IEC and WU values. Similarly, although V-2-O-1 and V-2-H-1 had similar IECs, the hydroxide conductivities of V-2-H-1 were superior due to better WU control. Encouragingly, the hydroxide conductivities of V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes exceeded 100 mS/cm at 40 °C (108, 112 and 114 mS/cm for V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1 and V-2-H-1, respectively) and exceeded 190 mS/cm at 90 °C (191, 195 and 199 mS/cm for V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1 and V-2-H-1, respectively), which were attributed to their high IEC and good water management properties. The Arrhenius plots of the hydroxide conduction indicated that the apparent activation energy values (E _{a}) were within the range of 7.6–12.6 kJ/mol (Fig. 3c and d) [39]. The E _{a} values of the highly conductive samples (V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1) were all about 10.6 kJ/mol, which were slightly lower than the previously reported diamine-cross-linked VA-PNB-AEMs (11.7–14.9) kJ/mol [39].

More detailed characterizations on the V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes were then performed to assist understanding the influence of water uptake on the AEM properties (Fig. 4 ). The WU and SR of the membranes at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 4a and b, respectively. Although the IECs of the AEMs were very high (up to 2.97 mmol/g), the membranes remained low WU and SR even at high temperatures (with WU less than 60% and SR less than 15% at 90 °C). This was attributed to the dithiol-cross-link, which helped maintaining the dimensional stability and integrity of the membranes. The WU and SR of V-1.5-O-1 were higher than those of V-1.5-H-1 because of the more hydrophilic cross-linker, and V-2-H-1 with the highest IECs also have the highest WU and SR among the three samples.

To further understand the water content in the membranes, the contents of free water (N _{free}) and bound water (N _{bound}) in the AEMs were studied using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) freezing point measurements (Fig. 4d) [26]. Excess water in the form of free water can lead to poor AEM performance due to membrane softening and channel flooding. The N _{free} values in membranes V-1.5-O-1 and V-1.5-H-1 were significantly lower than their N _{bound} values. Even for membrane V-2-H-1, which had the highest water uptake, also showed less N _{free} than N _{bound}. Therefore, the cross-link between dithiols and vinyl groups from VA-PNBs successfully managed the water molecules to be mostly bound around cations in the AEMs.

Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) analysis was then used to study the phase-separated morphologies of the V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes (Fig. 5 ). The results showed that no scattering peaks were detected in the one-dimensional (1-D) SAXS profiles of these random copolymer membranes, no matter in the Br^{−} form or the I^{−} form, indicating the potential homogeneous morphology [53,54]. This is consistent with a previous report that block copolymers with a locally ordered monomer sequence are more likely to form long-range ordered structures than random copolymers [40]. Furthermore, no evident ordered morphology but isotropic and uniform morphology was observed in the transmission electron microscope (TEM) images obtained from V-2-H-1 slices at different locations (Fig. S7). The homogenous morphology in the images clearly indicates that the microphase separation is extremely weak or negligible in our samples, which is consistent with the 1-D SAXS profiles. The results are reasonable if the interaction of the cross-linking process on the microphase separation is considered, i.e., the formation of bonding in the rapid cross-linking reaction restricts the chain mobility and leads to poor contrast between the phase domains (or even unable to establish the phase domain). Therefore, the cross-linking strategy that can control excess water uptake allows high-conductivity AEMs to be achieved in the absence of microphase separation [55].

Mechanical strength is crucial to ensure the integrity of the AEMs under operating conditions. All of the three membranes (V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1) prepared herein showed excellent mechanical strength (Fig. 6 and Table S2) [46,56]. The high mechanical strength is attributed to the dithiol-cross-link and the use of VA-PNB copolymers, which maintain a rigid bicyclic norbornene motif along the polymer backbones. The breaking strength of the membranes was between 25 40 MPa, with a corresponding breaking strain of 20%–25% and high modulus (V-1.5-H-1 had the highest modulus of up to 400 MPa). By comparing V-1.5-H-1 with V-1.5-O-1, the use of hydrophobic all-carbon dithiol cross-linker resulted in membranes with both higher stress-at-break and higher modulus.

To evaluate the thermal stability of V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes, thermogravimetric analyses (TGA) were performed. The TGA results and the derivative thermogravimetry (DTG) curves are shown in Fig. 7 . These curves indicate that all the membranes exhibited no significant degradation below 200 °C, suggesting that they possess excellent thermal stability that meets the required operating temperature range of AEMWE (60–80 °C). Moreover, when DSC was applied to characterize V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes, no detectable glass-transition was identified below 200 °C (Figs. S8–S10), further proving their excellent thermal stability [57].

It is important to note that the alkaline stability of the AEMs is critical for their effective use in AEMWE, as it can directly affect their durability and performance over time. The alkaline stability of two AEMs (V-1.5-H-1 and V-2-H-1) was evaluated by soaking them in a 1 M KOH solution at 80 °C for 1200 h (Fig. 8 ). The bicarbonate conductivities of the membranes were measured at regular intervals, and the results showed that both membranes exhibited good alkaline stability, with 81% and 63% conductivity remaining for V-1.5-H-1 and V-2-H-1, respectively (Fig. 8a). By measuring the IEC change of the membranes before and after the alkaline stability testing, it was found that 88% and 74% IEC were remained for V-1.5-H-1 and V-2-H-1 membranes, respectively (Fig. 8b). It is worth noting that V-2-H-1, which had a higher ionic content than V-1.5-H-1, exhibited a faster drop in conductivity under the alkaline stability testing conditions. This may be due to its weaker mechanical strength and poorer water uptake control (). The FT-IR analysis on the membranes before and after the alkaline stability testing revealed that the basic structure of the membranes was not significantly influenced (Fig. 8c and d). This suggests that the cation degradation is likely the primary factor affecting alkaline stability of the AEMs.

The highly conductive V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes were then subjected to AEMWE assembly for device performance evaluation [58,59]. The membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs) were fabricated using the catalyst-coated substrate (CCS) method, with the membranes sandwiched between two commercial, noble-metal-free electrodes [51]. Specifically, a NiFe_{2}O_{4} on stainless steel anode and NiFeCo on Ni fiber mat cathode were used. The polarization curves for V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 were measured in 1 M KOH at 60 °C, and the results are shown in Fig. 9 a. At an applied cell voltage of 2.0 V, the MEAs achieved electrolytic currents of 0.868 A cm^{−2}, 0.513 A cm^{−2}, and 0.868 A cm^{−2} for V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1, respectively. When the KOH concentration was reduced to 0.1 M, which is a more industrially appropriate concentration [60], the MEAs could still operate smoothly, producing current densities of 0.601 A cm^{−2}, 0.217 A cm^{−2}, and 0.567 A cm^{−2} at 2.0 V cell voltage for V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1, respectively (Fig. 9b). In addition, the current densities of the MEA assembled from membranes V-1.5-O-1 and V-2-H-1 were significantly better than that of commercial membrane PiperION A80 (0.32 A cm^{−2} at 2.0 V) in 0.1 M KOH at 60 °C (Fig. S11) [61]. The current densities of V-1.5-O-1 and V-2-H-1 were comparable both in 1 M KOH and in 0.1 M KOH, and the polarization curves of V-2-H-1 in 1 M KOH at various temperatures are shown in Fig. 9c. The current density of AEMWE was higher at 60 °C and 80 °C than at 40 °C. Durability tests of AEMWE were conducted with 0.1 M KOH electrolyte at 60 °C under constant current mode of 200 mA cm^{−2} (Fig. 9d–f). The average voltage increment rates for V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 assembled MEAs were measured to be 3.263 mV/h, 3.190 mV/h, and 3.363 mV/h, respectively, which could be attributed to the stability and compatibility of electrocatalysts, membranes, and interfaces [1,5]. The V-1.5-H-1 membrane assembled MEAs had the lowest voltage increment rates owing to its optimal alkaline stability at lower current density. Therefore, the dithiol-cross-linked VA-PNB-AEMs with high conductivities and excellent alkaline stabilities were successfully applied in AEMWEs, and the AEMWEs exhibited stable operation for more than 70 h.

Sections.name: Conclusion
content: In this study, a series of VA-PNB copolymers containing BrNB and VNB were synthesized using a three-component catalytic system of Pd_{2}(dba)_{3}, PCy_{3}, and Li[FABA]. The commercially available VNB monomer undergoes vinylic-addition copolymerization and the terminal alkene groups can be used for subsequent transformation. The copolymers were then photo-cross-linked with dithiol under UV irradiation and were quaternized to result in cross-linked VA-PNB-AEMs. A high percentage of BrNB can be inserted into the copolymer and the extent of cross-linking and the hydrophobicity of the cross-linkers can be easily controlled. Therefore, the copolymers allow for independent tuning of IEC, cross-linking degree, and the identity of the cross-linkers, resulting in AEMs with ultrahigh IECs and hydroxide conductivities. Specifically, the hydroxide conductivities of V-1.5-O-1, V-1.5-H-1, and V-2-H-1 membranes exceeded 100 mS/cm at 40 °C and 190 mS/cm at 90 °C. The crosslinked membranes showed low water uptake and swelling ratios even at high temperatures and IECs due to the contribution of the dithiol crosslinking agent. Compared to the O-containing cross-linker (3,6-dioxa-1,8-octanedithiol), the all-carbon cross-linker (1,6-hexanedithiol) demonstrated better water management. Additionally, the V-1.5-H-1 membrane exhibited good alkaline stability in 1 M KOH at 80 °C for 1200 h and stable AEWME performance, likely due to reasonable management of water molecules and excellent thermal stability.

Abstract: Vinylic-addition polynorbornenes possess high thermal stability, excellent mechanical integrity, and chemically inert backbones. Herein, we conveniently synthesize a series of vinylic-addition polynorbornene copolymers containing pendant alkenes from commercial vinyl-substituted norbornene (VNB) and alkyl-bromide-substituted norbornene (BrNB). Subsequently, the copolymers are photo-crosslinked with dithiol reagents through UV-initiated thiol-ene click reactions followed by quaternization to prepare the cross-linked anion-exchange membranes (AEMs). The extent of cross-linking and the hydrophobicity of the cross-linkers can be easily controlled, so that the absorption of excess water can be inhibited with enhanced membrane strength. The resultant AEMs have ultrahigh hydroxide conductivities (up to 199 mS/cm at 90 °C under humidified conditions) and excellent alkaline stability in 1 M KOH at 80 °C for 1200 h. The vinylic-addition AEMs are also successfully applied in alkaline anion-exchange membrane water electrolyzers with commercial noble-metal-free electrocatalysts.
